steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Add an import statement at the top of your file to import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the ES6 import syntax with curly braces to import multiple named exports from the same module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use in your component.
successCriteria: The import statement uses the correct package name 'react'
Both React and useState are imported
The syntax follows ES6 import conventions
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the state management hook you'll need for conditional rendering.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your import syntax. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package using the correct ES6 import syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start with the basics. You need to import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package using ES6 import syntax. This is essential for building React components with TypeScript.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX. The component should be defined with TypeScript and return a JSX element.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Remember to include the return type annotation.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named App is created with proper TypeScript syntax that returns JSX.
successCriteria: Component named 'App' is defined
Component returns JSX
Component has proper TypeScript syntax (explicit or inferred return type)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component with TypeScript. The component is ready to contain our conditional rendering logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the component 'App'? Does it return JSX? Is the TypeScript syntax correct?
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't properly defined. Make sure to create a functional component named App that returns JSX with TypeScript syntax.

steps.title: Initialize state for conditional rendering
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, declare a state variable called 'isLoggedIn' using useState, initialized to false. Make sure to use TypeScript's generic type annotation for boolean.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to specify the type as boolean with useState<boolean>(false).
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of declaring a boolean state variable
const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now has a boolean state variable 'isLoggedIn' initialized to false, ready to control conditional rendering.
successCriteria: useState hook is called
State variable is named 'isLoggedIn'
Initial value is false
TypeScript boolean type is specified with useState<boolean>
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the isLoggedIn state variable. This boolean will control what content gets rendered based on the user's login status.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the variable 'isLoggedIn'? Did you initialize it to false? Did you include the TypeScript boolean type annotation?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the App component, use useState<boolean>(false) to create a state variable called 'isLoggedIn'. This will be the condition for our ternary operator later.

steps.title: Define the toggle handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function called handleToggle that toggles the isLoggedIn state between true and false.
steps.hint: You can use the setter function from useState to update the state. Remember to use the previous state value to toggle.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleToggle function that toggles the isLoggedIn state when called.
successCriteria: The function should be named handleToggle and should update the isLoggedIn state using setIsLoggedIn.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined a toggle handler function that will flip the isLoggedIn state between true and false.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your handleToggle function properly toggles the state. It should use setIsLoggedIn with a function that returns the opposite of the previous state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleToggle function isn't defined correctly. It should toggle the isLoggedIn state using setIsLoggedIn.

steps.title: Add the main container div
steps.instruction: Inside your App component's return statement, add a <div> element that will wrap all the UI content you'll add later. Place it inside the existing outer <div>.
steps.hint: Add a <div> element after the <h1> tag. This will be the main container for your conditional rendering content.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a main container <div> ready to hold the conditional rendering content.
successCriteria: Add a <div> element inside the existing outer <div>
Place the new <div> after the <h1> element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the main container div that will hold your conditional rendering content.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added a <div> element inside the existing outer <div>, after the <h1>.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add a <div> element inside the existing outer <div> to serve as the main container for your conditional rendering content.

steps.title: Add a heading to explain the lesson
steps.instruction: Inside the main container div, add an h2 element with text that explains what this component demonstrates about conditional rendering with ternary operators.
steps.hint:
Add a heading element like

Some explanatory text here

inside the existing div container.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a heading to explain the component's purpose

This component shows how to conditionally render content using a ternary operator.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a second heading that explains the lesson's purpose, making the UI more informative.
successCriteria: Add an h2 element with explanatory text about conditional rendering with ternary operators inside the main div container.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added an explanatory heading to help users understand what this component demonstrates.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added an h2 element with text explaining conditional rendering with ternary operators.
steps.feedbackWrong: The heading wasn't added correctly. Add an h2 element with explanatory text about conditional rendering with ternary operators inside the main div container.

steps.title: Implement conditional rendering with ternary operator
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your component, add a paragraph element that uses the ternary operator to show different messages based on the current value of the isLoggedIn state.
steps.hint: The ternary operator syntax is: condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse. Use isLoggedIn as the condition, and render different text strings for true and false cases.
steps.expectedOutcome: A paragraph element that conditionally displays different text based on whether isLoggedIn is true or false.
successCriteria:
The code should include a

element with a ternary operator using isLoggedIn as the condition, showing one message when true and another when false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented conditional rendering using the ternary operator. The paragraph now shows different messages based on the isLoggedIn state value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your ternary operator syntax. Make sure you have: isLoggedIn ? 'message when true' : 'message when false' inside the paragraph element.
steps.feedbackWrong:
The paragraph with ternary operator isn't implemented correctly. Remember to use the syntax: {isLoggedIn ? 'text for true' : 'text for false'} inside a

element.

steps.title: Add the toggle button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Toggle Login Status' inside the main container div, and wire its onClick event to the handleToggle function.
steps.hint: Place the button after the heading and paragraph. Use the onClick prop to call handleToggle when the button is clicked.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a button with onClick handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Toggle Status</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Toggle Login Status' appears below the paragraph, and clicking it toggles the login status message between 'You are logged in!' and 'You are logged out.'
successCriteria: Button element with text 'Toggle Login Status'
onClick prop set to handleToggle function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the toggle button and wired it to the handler. The button will now toggle the login status when clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have both: 1) a button with the exact text 'Toggle Login Status', and 2) the onClick prop set to handleToggle.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly configured. Check that you have a button element with the text 'Toggle Login Status' and its onClick is set to handleToggle.

steps.title: Add a second conditional render with different content
steps.instruction: Add another ternary operator inside the return statement that renders different button styles based on the isLoggedIn state. The ternary should conditionally set the button's className to either 'btn-logged-in' or 'btn-logged-out'.
steps.hint: You can add this ternary directly in the className attribute of the button element. Use the same isLoggedIn state variable as before.
steps.expectedOutcome: The button will have a dynamic className that changes between 'btn-logged-in' and 'btn-logged-out' based on the isLoggedIn state.
successCriteria: The button element should include a className attribute with a ternary operator that uses isLoggedIn to conditionally return 'btn-logged-in' or 'btn-logged-out'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a second conditional render using a ternary operator to dynamically change the button's className based on the isLoggedIn state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the ternary operator is correctly implemented in the button's className attribute. It should use isLoggedIn to conditionally return 'btn-logged-in' or 'btn-logged-out'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button doesn't have a conditional className using a ternary operator. Remember to add className={isLoggedIn ? 'btn-logged-in' : 'btn-logged-out'} to the button element.

steps.title: Export the App component
steps.instruction: Export the App component as the default export so it can be imported and used in other files.
steps.hint: Add the export statement at the bottom of the file. Use 'export default' followed by the component name.
steps.analogousExample:
// Export a component as default
export default App;
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is properly exported as the default export, making it available for import in other modules.
successCriteria: The file contains an export default statement
The export default statement references the App component
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully exported the App component as the default export. This makes the component available for use in other files when imported.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the export statement isn't quite complete. Make sure you're using 'export default' followed by the component name 'App'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The export statement is missing or incorrect. Remember to add 'export default App;' at the bottom of the file to make the component available for import.
